newsitem.title: USA: Clinton sending landmines team to Europe.
newsitem.headline: Clinton sending landmines team to Europe.

text.p: President Bill Clinton is sending a team of senior officials to Geneva this week to weigh in on international negotiations to ban landmines, administration officials said.
The White House was due to announce its plans on Monday.

The officials, who declined to be identified, said the delegation would confer with representatives of countries pushing under the leadership of Canada for an alternative treaty, signalling new readiness by the White House to consider the so-called Ottawa process.

"The administration has decided on a ... new policy that will hopefully move the process toward the president's goal of a global ban on anti-personnel landmines that protects military interests," one official said.

The official said it would be premature to say Clinton had decided to endorse the Canadian initiative, which promises a treaty by the end of the year banning the use, export, production and stockpiling of anti-personnel land mines.
"I think that would be a little ahead of the game," the official said. "We're not quite ready to endorse the Ottowa process."
But the delegation heading to Europe would gather information about the negotiations under way in Geneva and try to determine "where they are, where does the process go from here," the official said.
Canada is anxiously awaiting a decision on whether Clinton will throw his weight behind its initiative for a worldwide ban on landmines.
Canada's special representative on landmines, John English, said in Ottawa on Friday: "It would be a very, very good thing if they would come around."

Laborious discussions in Geneva on a landmine ban have failed to make much progress, but Canada's invitation to meet in Ottawa and sign a treaty outlawing landmines later this year has drawn the backing of major U.S. allies.

The U.N.-sponsored conference in Geneva in May 1996 agreed to limit the use of some landmines but stopped short of a total ban because some countries argue they should remain a legitimate form of defense. Over 100 countries -- but not the United States -- have agreed to a total ban.
U.S. federal health officials estimated earlier this month that 9,600 people are killed by landmines worldwide every year and another 14,000 are wounded, double the number of injuries logged in 1980.
The administration officials said Clinton decided to send his team on a "fact-finding" mission after completion of a U.S. interagency review on the issue.
"We think we want to continue the diplomatic process," one official said.

U.S. officials will seek to bridge the gaps between the two parallel negotiating tracks -- the Ottawa process and the official U.N. negotiations in Geneva -- in hopes of finding a "more successful route," the official said.
"Basically they will be taking stock of Ottawa and seeing if that meshes more with where we want to end up," the official said.

The U.S. delegation is headed by Robert Bell, senior director for defense and military affairs at the National Security Council, and includes other senior officials from White House, the State Department and the Pentagon.

Clinton rejected the Canadian initiative in January after concluding it left little room for exceptions sought by U.S. military commanders. U.S. officials have also noted that such a total ban would have little impact without the endorsement of China and Russia, the world's biggest producers of landmines.
Countries involved in the Ottawa process will meet for a three-week drafting of a final text in Oslo from Sept. 1.
